Extinct
eks-tinkt'
adj. (put out, quenched; used of a man's days at the end of life and of an army snuffed out like a wick)
Latin exstinctus, past participle of exstinguere, to quench or put out. The image in both biblical uses is a flame that has gone out, not a species that has died away — the modern biological sense is later.

Biblical Definition

Job, at the lowest point of his complaint, says: “My breath is corrupt, my days are extinct, the graves are ready for me” (Job 17:1). The figure is a lamp burning down — the days are not stolen but spent, and the wick is out. He adds in the next breath, “Are there not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation?” (Job 17:2), so the extinction he feels is aggravated by comforters who will not comfort. Isaiah uses the word of the destruction of Egypt's army at the sea: the LORD “bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow” (Isaiah 43:17). Quenched as tow is a striking picture — tow is the coarse fibre of flax, which flares up and is gone. The whole force of Pharaoh's chariotry is a handful of burning tow before the God who “maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters” (Isaiah 43:16). And Isaiah's purpose in recalling it is not nostalgia: the next verse tells them to remember it no more, for He will do a new thing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines extinct as extinguished, put out, quenched, and also as having no survivor or being at an end.

expand to see more

EXTINCT, a. Extinguished; put out; quenched; as, a fire, a light or a lamp is extinct.

2. Being at an end; having no survivor; as, a family or race is extinct.

3. Being at an end; having ceased.

EXTINGUISH, v.t. To put out; to quench; to suffocate; to destroy; as, to extinguish fire or flame.

TOW, n. The coarse and broken part of flax or hemp, separated from the finer part by the hatchel.

Key Scripture

Job 17:1 — "My breath is corrupt, my days are extinct, the graves are ready for me."

Isaiah 43:17 — "Which bringeth forth the chariot and horse, the army and the power; they shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow."

Isaiah 43:16 — "Thus saith the LORD, which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters;"

Job 17:2 — "Are there not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation?"

Modern Corruption

The despair of a righteous sufferer is treated as a failure of faith to be corrected, when Scripture records it without rebuke.

expand to see more

Job 17:1 is the kind of verse that embarrasses a certain sort of piety. A righteous man says his days are burnt out and the graves are ready for him, and no narrator steps in to correct him. Scripture is willing to record the speech of a saint at the end of his resources, and the book of Job exists partly to show that the comforters, who had a tidy explanation for everything, were the ones God rebuked. A church that permits no such speech, and treats every expression of anguish as unbelief to be talked out of, has adopted the theology of Eliphaz while quoting the words of Job. The Psalms are full of the same register, and the darkest of them ends without resolution.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what Isaiah does with the word. He recalls the greatest deliverance in the nation's history — the chariots quenched as tow — and then tells them to remember it no more, because God is about to do a new thing. Memory of past mercy is not the goal; it is the ground for expecting present mercy. Congregations that live entirely on the recollection of a former season, and congregations that despise the past altogether, have each taken half of Isaiah 43 and left the half that corrects them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zaak, to be extinguished — Job 17:1; daak, to go out or be quenched — Isaiah 43:17; neoreth, tow — Isaiah 43:17.

expand to see more

Hebrew zaak — to be extinguished, snuffed out; Job 17:1, of a man's days.

Hebrew daak — to go out, be quenched; Isaiah 43:17, and Proverbs 13:9 of the lamp of the wicked.

Hebrew neoreth — tow, the coarse fibre of flax; Isaiah 43:17, and Judges 16:9 of the cords Samson snapped.

Hebrew qeber — a grave; Job 17:1, in the plural, the graves are ready for me.

Isaiah 43:18-19 supplies the turn: remember ye not the former things, for behold, I will do a new thing.

Usage

"“My days are extinct, the graves are ready for me” — recorded without rebuke."

"“They are extinct, they are quenched as tow” — Pharaoh's chariots as burning flax."

"The figure is a wick gone out, not a species died away."
